section_summary: This section documents efforts to revive Japanese textile production and exports after the war, alongside concerns about competition, raw materials, financing, and access to foreign markets. Correspondence and reports cover cotton, rayon, textile machinery, and domestic clothing shortages. Several documents record opposition from American, British, and Chinese textile interests, while State Department officials argue that textile exports are necessary for Japan’s economic recovery.

subfiles.title: Continuation of reply concerning entry into Japan
subfiles.about: The Department reports that SCAP will consider entry requests from three commission members.
subfiles.summary: SCAP’s decision on Kavadar, Aydimelli, and Sipaki will be relayed to the embassy.

subfiles.title: Availability of Japanese and German Cotton Textiles for Yemen
subfiles.about: The Jidda legation forwards correspondence with Yemen about textile purchases.
subfiles.summary: Childs encloses his offer, Yemen’s reply, and his acknowledgment.

subfiles.title: Offer of Japanese and German textiles to Yemen
subfiles.about: The United States offers limited Japanese and German textiles for dollar purchase.
subfiles.summary: Childs explains available cloth and yarn, pricing, allocation priorities, and the need for prompt estimates of Yemeni requirements.

subfiles.title: Yemen’s reply on textile purchases
subfiles.about: Yemen says merchants cannot meet the proposed dollar-payment timetable.
subfiles.summary: The foreign minister cites difficulty obtaining dollars and says merchants will extend their orders over a longer period.

subfiles.title: Clarification to Yemen on textile purchases
subfiles.about: Childs corrects Yemen’s understanding of the proposed purchase amount.
subfiles.summary: He says his earlier note specified no two-million-dollar sum and offers further assistance.

subfiles.title: Inquiry into cotton procurement for Japan
subfiles.about: Knowland asks whether Japan will buy cotton from India, Brazil, and the United States.
subfiles.summary: He requests details of negotiations, financing, timing, and prospective American cotton exports.

subfiles.title: Reply to Senator Knowland on Japanese cotton procurement
subfiles.from: Durward V. Sandifer for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department explains its policy on supplying raw cotton to occupied Japan.
subfiles.summary: It expects a substantial American share while recognizing other cotton exporters’ access to Japan and seeking equitable procurement.

subfiles.title: Internal routing note on a reply
subfiles.about: An office note discusses a letter awaiting signature.
subfiles.summary: The writer believes the letter requires no reply.

subfiles.title: Cotton-Textile Institute follow-up
subfiles.about: Planz requests the State Department’s reaction to the institute’s presentation.
subfiles.summary: He reports a detailed discussion with Martin and asks for the government’s response.

subfiles.title: Inquiry into Japanese textile sales in Siam
subfiles.about: The Department requests information about Siamese purchases of Japanese textiles.
subfiles.summary: It asks about quality, use, and likely future orders.

subfiles.title: British parliamentary answer on Japanese cotton mills
subfiles.about: The embassy reports British parliamentary figures for Japan’s cotton industry.
subfiles.summary: The answer gives spindle, loom, and employment figures.

subfiles.title: British parliamentary answer on Japanese automatic looms
subfiles.about: The embassy reports plans for British imports of Japanese automatic looms.
subfiles.summary: No looms had arrived; arrangements were underway to import 192.

subfiles.title: Japanese textiles sold in Siam
subfiles.about: The embassy reports distribution, quality complaints, and future prospects for Japanese textiles.
subfiles.summary: Poor quality and depleted Siamese dollar reserves make further cash purchases unlikely.

subfiles.title: A Provisional Survey of Japan’s Textile Industry
subfiles.about: A survey estimates textile requirements and the industry’s prospects for recovery.
subfiles.summary: Production and domestic consumption remain far below prewar levels. The memorandum emphasizes textile exports as a source of foreign exchange and provides consumption and yarn-production tables.

subfiles.title: Kohorn transmittal of rayon-program criticism
subfiles.about: Frick forwards the company’s proposed criticism of Japan’s rayon program.
subfiles.summary: He offers to keep the State Department informed.

subfiles.title: Critique of the rayon production program for Japan
subfiles.about: Kohorn challenges the efficiency assumptions of SCAP’s rayon production plan.
subfiles.summary: Frick argues that projected output per spindle is too low, raw-material use too high, and machinery plans poorly balanced. He recommends an engineering review and offers company experts.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Kohorn’s rayon-program letter
subfiles.about: Whitman acknowledges receipt of Kohorn’s criticism.
subfiles.summary: He says the comments will interest State and SCAP officials.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of SCAP textile-allocation announcement
subfiles.about: The adviser forwards SCAP’s announcement on increased domestic textile allocations.
subfiles.summary: Five copies of the October 15 announcement are enclosed.

subfiles.title: SCAP press release on textile allocations and other news
subfiles.about: SCAP announces greater textile allocations for Japanese consumers.
subfiles.summary: The release raises cotton-yarn allocations for domestic use and describes releases of silk, rayon, and clothing for essential groups. Its later pages contain unrelated announcements on weather, congressional visitors, sport, war-crimes proceedings, and a military appointment.

subfiles.title: Kohorn transmittal of further rayon correspondence
subfiles.about: Frick forwards another letter to the Army on Japanese rayon production.
subfiles.summary: The letter encloses Kohorn’s renewed proposal.

subfiles.title: Renewed proposal for engineering review of Japanese rayon
subfiles.about: Kohorn again urges more efficient rayon production and offers experts.
subfiles.summary: Frick cites the shortage and rising price of rayon pulp. He proposes a preliminary engineering survey at no cost apart from travel and subsistence.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Kohorn’s second rayon letter
subfiles.about: Whitman acknowledges Kohorn’s views on reviving Japan’s rayon industry.
subfiles.summary: He thanks Frick for providing the November 6 letter.

subfiles.title: Inquiry into Japanese loom production
subfiles.about: Leeson questions reports that Japan produced more looms than U.S. manufacturers.
subfiles.summary: He encloses a letter and corrected news story and asks whether the figures accord with SCAP policy.

subfiles.title: West’s challenge to a loom-production report
subfiles.about: West questions a report of 2,400 Japanese looms produced in October.
subfiles.summary: He suggests the reported figure might instead represent repaired looms.

subfiles.title: Corrected report on Japanese loom production
subfiles.about: The corrected story reports new looms and repaired looms separately.
subfiles.summary: It reports 2,593 new looms and 789 repaired or rebuilt in October.

subfiles.title: Reply on Japanese textile-machinery production
subfiles.about: Whitman confirms substantial Japanese loom production and explains SCAP policy.
subfiles.summary: He says Japan may produce machinery for domestic needs and export; restoring peaceful industry and trade is part of making Japan self-supporting.

subfiles.title: Leeson’s acknowledgment
subfiles.about: Leeson thanks Whitman for his explanation.
subfiles.summary: He acknowledges Whitman’s March 24 letter.

subfiles.title: British parliamentary exchange on Japanese textile policy
subfiles.about: The embassy forwards parliamentary questions about Japanese textile production and Lancashire competition.
subfiles.summary: British ministers discuss production controls, labor standards, and the competitive position of Lancashire.

subfiles.title: Draft telegram correcting Chinese account of Japanese textiles
subfiles.about: The Department drafts corrections to claims about Japanese textile policy.
subfiles.summary: It says textiles are outside reparations, American cotton is supplied on credit, and China may receive machinery through barter.

subfiles.title: Revised telegram on Japanese textile policy
subfiles.about: A revised message supplies facts for rebutting a Chinese article.
subfiles.summary: It explains reparations policy, cotton credit, indigenous rehabilitation materials, and spindle needs for domestic consumption.

subfiles.title: Partly illegible incoming airgram
subfiles.about: The surviving OCR does not establish the airgram’s subject reliably.
subfiles.summary: Most substantive text is illegible.

subfiles.title: Inquiry into a Japanese market for American textile machinery
subfiles.about: A machinery maker asks whether Japan needs imported equipment.
subfiles.summary: Schaberg asks about Japanese capacity and a reported contract to supply spindles to India.

subfiles.title: Reply on Japanese textile-machinery capacity
subfiles.about: Penfield assesses prospects for selling American textile machinery in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Japan’s surviving capacity meets domestic needs and supports exports, including spindles for India. Penfield sees little near-term market for imported machinery.

subfiles.title: Comments on Japanese textile-industry prospects
subfiles.about: A memorandum surveys foreign reactions to Japanese textiles.
subfiles.summary: It notes costly Japanese cloth for India, Chinese and British concern about competition, changing export markets, and Australian wool financing.

subfiles.title: Kohorn proposal for a Chinese rayon industry
subfiles.about: Frick proposes Chinese rayon production in place of large dollar purchases of Japanese rayon.
subfiles.summary: He argues that a $3 million plant could reduce China’s import costs and support its textile and export industries. Kohorn offers further technical advice.

subfiles.title: Reply on China’s rayon needs
subfiles.about: The Department responds to Kohorn’s Chinese rayon proposal.
subfiles.summary: Aid funds are not planned for Japanese rayon imports; the plant proposal is forwarded for possible future use.

subfiles.title: Background on J & P Coats interests in Japan
subfiles.about: The memorandum assesses restoration of Coats’s wartime-damaged Japanese operations.
subfiles.summary: Coats’s equipment was destroyed, and compensation policy remains unsettled. Renting idle Japanese equipment is suggested as a route to renewed production.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Walker’s letter
subfiles.about: Kohorn acknowledges the Department’s response on Chinese rayon.
subfiles.summary: Frick’s office says his letter will be shown to him on his return.

subfiles.title: Shanghai commercial opposition to American aid to Japan
subfiles.about: Pilcher reports a Chinese article opposing revival of Japan’s textile industry.
subfiles.summary: He links anti-aid agitation to Shanghai commercial interests, particularly textiles. The article portrays Japanese textile recovery as a threat to China and alleges American business sponsorship.

subfiles.title: Continuation of conversation on Japanese textile restrictions
subfiles.about: A surviving continuation records discussion with American textile representatives.
subfiles.summary: Industry representatives warn of Japanese competition. Martin argues that textile exports are essential to paying for Japan’s imports and are unsuitable for arbitrary limits.

subfiles.title: Routing note on textile-industry meeting
subfiles.about: Fearey forwards a conversation memorandum and comments on industry demands.
subfiles.summary: He strongly opposes limiting Japan’s principal peaceful industry.

subfiles.title: Policy regarding Japanese Textile Industry
subfiles.about: Officials and textile representatives debate limits on Japanese cotton production.
subfiles.summary: American industry representatives describe market pressure and seek a ceiling on Japanese production. Martin argues that exports are necessary for Japan to pay for imports and regain economic stability; the surviving copy is partly illegible.

subfiles.title: Document charge slip
subfiles.about: A form records the charging of a letter from the file.
subfiles.summary: The form has limited legible identifying information.

subfiles.title: Reply concerning Japanese textile-machinery prices
subfiles.about: Noonan thanks Whitman for production data and raises export-price concerns.
subfiles.summary: His association finds Japanese machinery prices generally below American and British prices and may seek further advice.

subfiles.title: Shanghai report on opposition to Japanese textile revival
subfiles.about: The consulate reports another protest against rebuilding Japan’s textile industry.
subfiles.summary: The damaged OCR indicates Chinese opposition to expanding Japanese spindle capacity and calls for restrictions or reparations.
